item.title: Matching Carbon Monoxide Absorptions to Molecular Transitions
item.stimulus:
A sample of carbon monoxide gas, CO(g), is placed in a sealed cell. The cell is exposed in turn to three radiation sources. Each source emits one wavelength, and CO absorbs strongly at each wavelength. The data are shown below.

Source | Wavelength of radiation absorbed by CO(g)
A | 2.60 mm
B | 4.67 μm
C | 155 nm

Useful information: h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s; N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. The bond enthalpy of the carbon–oxygen triple bond in CO is 1072 kJ/mol.
item.model_answer:
(a) Source A, 2.60 mm = 2.60 × 10⁻³ m, is microwave radiation. Absorbing it causes CO to change to a higher rotational energy level. Source B, 4.67 μm = 4.67 × 10⁻⁶ m, is infrared radiation. Absorbing it causes CO to change to a higher vibrational energy level.

(b) E = hc/λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)(2.998 × 10⁸ m/s)/(4.67 × 10⁻⁶ m) = 4.25 × 10⁻²⁰ J.

(c) Source C (155 nm) is ultraviolet radiation and causes an electronic transition, promoting an electron in CO to a higher electronic energy level. Because E = hc/λ, the shortest wavelength gives the greatest photon energy: E_C = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴)(2.998 × 10⁸)/(155 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, compared with 4.25 × 10⁻²⁰ J for B and 7.64 × 10⁻²³ J for A. Electronic energy levels are spaced much farther apart than vibrational or rotational levels, so only the highest-energy photons from source C can cause an electronic transition.

(d) I disagree. Energy of one source A photon: E = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴)(2.998 × 10⁸)/(2.60 × 10⁻³ m) = 7.64 × 10⁻²³ J. Energy to break one C≡O bond: (1072 × 10³ J/mol)/(6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) = 1.78 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. The photon energy is about 2.33 × 10⁴ times smaller than the energy needed to break the bond, so absorbing a microwave photon only raises the rotational energy of CO; the bond does not break.
item.verification_python:
import math
h=6.626e-34
c=2.998e8
NA=6.022e23
EA=h*c/2.60e-3
EB=h*c/4.67e-6
EC=h*c/155e-9
bond=1072e3/NA
assert abs(EB-4.25e-20)/4.25e-20<0.002
assert abs(EA-7.64e-23)/7.64e-23<0.002
assert abs(EC-1.28e-18)/1.28e-18<0.003
assert abs(bond-1.78e-18)/1.78e-18<0.002
ratio=bond/EA
assert abs(ratio-2.33e4)/2.33e4<0.003
assert abs(EA*NA-46.0)<0.1
assert EC>EB>EA
assert EC<bond
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

parts.prompt: Identify the region of the electromagnetic spectrum for source A and for source B. For each, identify the type of molecular transition in CO that results when the photon is absorbed.

criteria.text: Source A (2.60 mm) is microwave radiation, and its absorption causes a transition between rotational energy levels of CO.
criteria.evidence: States that source A is microwave and that absorbing it changes the rotational energy level of the CO molecule.
criteria.fix: Memorize the pairings: microwave changes rotational levels, infrared changes vibrational levels, UV/visible changes electronic levels.

criteria.text: Source B (4.67 μm) is infrared radiation, and its absorption causes a transition between vibrational energy levels of CO.
criteria.evidence: States that source B is infrared and that absorbing it changes the vibrational energy level (bond stretching) of the CO molecule.
criteria.fix: Convert micrometers to meters, place 10⁻⁶ m in the infrared region, then pair infrared with vibrational transitions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the energy, in joules, of one photon emitted by source B.

criteria.evidence: Shows the setup using E = hc/λ (or c = λν and E = hν) with the wavelength converted to 4.67 × 10⁻⁶ m, and reports 4.25 × 10⁻²⁰ J with units.
criteria.fix: Convert the wavelength to meters first, then substitute into E = hc/λ and report three significant figures with units.

parts.prompt: Identify the type of transition in CO caused by absorption of a photon from source C. Justify your answer by comparing the energy of a photon from source C with the energies of photons from sources A and B.

criteria.text: Source C (155 nm, ultraviolet) causes an electronic transition; it has the shortest wavelength and therefore the highest photon energy, matching the larger energy spacing between electronic levels compared with vibrational or rotational levels.
criteria.evidence: Identifies an electronic transition (electron promoted to a higher energy level) and justifies it by stating that the shortest wavelength gives the greatest photon energy (E = hc/λ), which is needed for the larger electronic energy gaps.
criteria.fix: Rank photon energies by wavelength using E = hc/λ, then link the highest-energy photons to electronic transitions, which have the largest spacing.
accepted_variants: promotes an electron to a higher energy level

parts.prompt: A student claims that when CO absorbs photons from source A, the carbon–oxygen bond breaks. Do you agree or disagree? Justify your answer with a calculation comparing the energy of one source A photon with the energy needed to break one C≡O bond.

criteria.text: Disagrees: one source A photon has E = hc/λ = 7.64 × 10⁻²³ J, far less than the 1.78 × 10⁻¹⁸ J needed to break one C≡O bond (1072 kJ/mol ÷ N_A), so absorption only changes the rotational energy level.
criteria.evidence: Disagrees with the claim and supports it with both calculated values (about 7.64 × 10⁻²³ J per photon and about 1.78 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per bond) or an equivalent per-mole comparison, concluding the photon energy is much too small to break the bond.
criteria.fix: Convert bond enthalpy to joules per molecule by dividing by Avogadro's number, then compare it directly with the energy of one photon.
accepted_variants: photon energy is about 2.33 × 10⁴ times too small
